newsitem.title: USA: Elections may boost balanced budget amendment.
newsitem.headline: Elections may boost balanced budget amendment.

text.p: Tuesday's elections appear to have provided the necessary votes for congressional approval of a balanced budget amendment to the Constitution, a review of the newly elected Senate showed Thursday.

The amendment appears to have the support of at least the 67 senators needed in the 100-member body. If it is approved by 38 state legislatures and becomes part of the Constitution -- the president's signature is not required -- the amendment promises a new fiscal era for the United States, which has balanced its budget only eight times in the past 66 years.

While almost all national politicians now favour balancing the budget by 2002 and many have offered plans to do so, President Clinton and a shrinking minority in Congress oppose enshrining such a requirement in the Constitution.

The proposed amendment easily passed the House, 300-132, last year and if past patterns hold would easily pass again, but it fell one vote short in the Senate. The elections have changed that by sending new balanced budget amendment supporters from both parties to the Senate.
A Reuters count shows that 67 members of the new Senate voted for the amendment when it was last before Congress or promised in their election campaigns to support it.

Among the key changes is New Jersey, where Democrat Robert Torricelli, who voted for the amendment in the House, replaces retiring Democratic Sen. Bill Bradley, who voted against it. Other newly elected Democrats who support a balanced budget amendment are Mary Landrieu of Louisiana, Max Cleland of Georgia and Tim Johnson of South Dakota.
Democrat Richard Durbin of Illinois, elected to replace Democrat Paul Simon, voted against the measure when he was in the House. Simon was one of the authors of the amendment.

The key vote last time was Republican Mark Hatfield of Oregon, who voted against the measure. Mail ballots have yet to decide whether he is replaced by a Republican who favours the amendment or a Demcorat who opposes it.

Proponents say that if the amendment passes it would force the government to shrink. That would likely affect the four big-ticket items that together make up two-thirds of government spending -- Social Security, the military, interest on the national debt and Medicare.
The amendment makes several technical but very basic changes in the Constitution that would raise new procedural hurdles in votes on the deficit and debt.

A three-fifths vote of all members would be required to permit a deficit, except in wartime, or to raise the debt limit. The debt limit, which now requires a simple majority vote for an increase, is something like the credit limit on a charge card. Failure to raise it could ultimately force the country to default on its debts.
The measure would also make it harder to raise taxes by requiring majorities of all members of both houses rather than just those voting and requiring recorded votes on such bills.
